subject: An idea for dealing with discrete parameters

messages.author: ee490f1373633c05
messages.subject: An idea for dealing with discrete parameters
parts:
As I understand it, one of the challenges with doing HMC on discrete parameters is that any sort of step function destroys the derivative information, making HMC very hard.

Perhaps there is some way to implement a trick quasi-step function that produces acceptable outputs.

For sample, suppose I have some contribution to the likelihood P(A | B) . P (B), where A is continuous and B is a discrete parameter.

For P(B), you could implement some almost step function, so that there is in fact an change in the gradient between B = i and B = i+1.

However, you could then use an actual step function for P(A | B) so that you are getting the correct likelihood contribution here.

Effectively, you are trying to run some latent/hidden process and map this back to the truly discrete parameter space when required.

An example

For example, consider the Poisson distribution.  Rather than using L = (lambda^k)*exp(-lambda)/k!, you could use the continuous approximation (lambda^k)*exp(-lambda)/Gamma(k+1), which is is valid for all continuous k.  If you then had some other function which depends on this Poission variable, you apply a step function to truncate back to being a discrete parameter.  Overall, the likelihood function will not be quite so badly behaved...

Alternatively, perhaps you just use continuous approximations to discrete parameters, and then do some kind of post-processing to (approximately) truncate to the discrete space for the output.

Thoughts?

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: An idea for dealing with discrete parameters
parts:
An example

For example, consider the Poisson distribution.  Rather than using L = (lambda^k)*exp(-lambda)/k!, you could use the continuous approximation (lambda^k)*exp(-lambda)/Gamma(k+1), which is is valid for all continuous k.  If you then had some other function which depends on this Poission variable, you apply a step function to truncate back to being a discrete parameter.  Overall, the likelihood function will not be quite so badly behaved...

The truncation will lead to a discontinuity in the gradient of the posterior, leading to a degenerate HMC. Mixture models are the ways to go (see Stan manual). Some people have tried to approximate step function with continuous versions, but only for one step, not multiple steps from integer to integer. I reckon the latter would be rather hard to sample from the posterior as it would be rather wobbly (depending on the amount of information in the data). Maybe others can comment on their experiences with approximating single step functions with a continuous function.

Alternatively, perhaps you just use continuous approximations to discrete parameters, and then do some kind of post-processing to (approximately) truncate to the discrete space for the output.

Thoughts?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An idea for dealing with discrete parameters
parts:
We've been thinking all along that what we'd do is
have a joint posterior

p(theta,z|y)

where theta are continuous and z discrete parameters.
It's kosher to do a Gibbs-like update of

p(theta|z,y)

and

p(z|theta,y).

The first one can be done with HMC, but the adaptation
needs to be redone each time because

p(theta|z,y) =/= p(theta|z', y).

Something like RHMC should help a lot here because it will
auto-tune for curvature and step size should be relatively
easy to adapt.

Then there's an issue of how to deal with the discrete
sampling p(z|theta). We could do Gibbs or Metropolis here,
but we don't have any easy way to compute this without
computing the whole joint probability function p(theta,z,y).
We haven't figured out a clever way to do the Markov blanket,
which would support Gibbs. More than one person has now
suggested analyzing the expression tree of the log probability function.
I haven't thought that through yet, perhaps because I'm put
off by the huge amount of work it would require.

Finally, I don't think anyone knows how well the whole
posterior will mix. Certainly not any better than the
discrete component p(z|theta,y) mixes.

- Bob

messages.author: 29f6a893ff2525e2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An idea for dealing with discrete parameters
parts:
It's a hard problem. One obvious difficulty with doing a Gibbs sampler for the discrete variables is that there is no reason to believe, if you change a discrete variable and keep the continuous variables fixed, that you will have anything like a decent likelihood, so it will always be rejected.

I deal with discrete geological models, and each model may have continuous change of permeability or porosity. But the permeability map for model 1 will often be very different to the permeability map for model 2.

It's the basic problem with Gibbs sampling, or indeed most sampling.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An idea for dealing with discrete parameters
parts: Does thinking about this in a mixture or stick-breaking framework help any?  re-parametrize theta_1,...,theta_N by group index, s_1,...,s_N and ``locations", theta^{*}_1,...,theta^{*}_N.  it somewhat de-couples updating the discrete assignments from moving the continuous locations.  Of course, the number of observations assigned to each continuous location will update in the sampler.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An idea for dealing with discrete parameters
parts:
> On Nov 7, 2014, at 12:39 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
>
> It's a hard problem. One obvious difficulty with doing a Gibbs sampler for the discrete variables is that there is no reason to believe, if you change a discrete variable and keep the continuous variables fixed, that you will have anything like a decent likelihood, so it will always be rejected.

Exactly --- that's the general problem with sampling
one variable at a time. The other way to look at it is
that you have to make small changes in order for them to
be accepted, which may lead to little or no mixing. But
with categorical, it's all or nothing if you change a variable.

> I deal with discrete geological models, and each model may have continuous change of permeability or porosity. But the permeability map for model 1 will often be very different to the permeability map for model 2.
>
> It's the basic problem with Gibbs sampling, or indeed most sampling.

The nice thing about HMC is that it can make coherent
long-distance proposals in high dimensions. But only with
continuous parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An idea for dealing with discrete parameters
parts:
I didn't follow the reparameterization. In general, theta
can be any sequence of parameters --- I tend to think of
stick-breaking as something to apply to unit simplexes (in
fact, it's the parameterization we use for them under the hood).

- Bob
